texts.label: A
texts.title: The curator
texts.text: A memorable museum does not merely display objects; it gives visitors a reason to connect them. I favour a clear narrative, even if that means leaving some material in storage. Without selection, a collection becomes an inventory, and an inventory rarely changes how anyone sees the world.

texts.label: B
texts.title: The architect
texts.text: I am less persuaded by narrative. Visitors should be able to make unexpected connections, so I prefer spaces that allow several routes through a collection. A well-designed room can be suggestive without telling people what to think.

texts.label: C
texts.title: The teacher
texts.text: The finest exhibitions respect the visitor’s time. I look for labels that answer genuine questions rather than display specialist vocabulary. A modest object can be powerful when its context is made accessible, but accessibility is not the same as simplifying everything.

texts.label: D
texts.title: The researcher
texts.text: Museums should be places of uncertainty. I become suspicious when an exhibition presents one interpretation as final. Evidence can be arranged clearly while still acknowledging gaps, disagreement and the possibility that new work will change the story.

questions.prompt: Which writer values presenting a coherent storyline?
questions.explanation: The curator explicitly favours a clear narrative and purposeful selection.

questions.prompt: Which writer believes visitors should have freedom to form their own links?
questions.explanation: The architect prefers several routes and unexpected connections rather than a prescribed narrative.

questions.prompt: Which writer distinguishes accessibility from making content simplistic?
questions.explanation: The teacher says accessibility is not the same as simplifying everything.

questions.prompt: Which writer stresses that interpretations may need revision?
questions.explanation: The researcher refers to new work changing the story and warns against final interpretations.
